did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah describes the heavens as the LORD’s throne and the earth as his footstool, emphasizing that no house or temple can contain the fullness of his greatness.

Did you know? Although the LORD created everything, he looks especially to the poor, the brokenhearted, and those who tremble at his word—in other words, to the humble and those attentive to his divine command.
Did you know? The chapter teaches that sacrifices and religious practices are not acceptable when they are accompanied by evil deeds and a deliberate choice to follow ways the LORD opposes.

Did you know? Isaiah describes a time when those who honor the word of the LORD are rejected and persecuted by their own brothers, who even portray them as acting against the LORD’s honor; in the end, according to the prophecy, the persecutors will be put to shame.
Did you know? Zion is portrayed as giving birth to a son before her labor pains begin, emphasizing the suddenness and speed of redemption.

Did you know? Jerusalem is presented as a mother with whom people should rejoice, especially after a period of mourning over her; rejoicing in Jerusalem is portrayed as a response to her comfort and restoration.
Did you know? The abundance of redemption is described through images of a river of peace, a stream of glory, and nursing—pictures expressing security, nourishment, and prosperity in Jerusalem.
Did you know? After the judgment, the LORD sends survivors to distant nations, including Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, and Greece, to proclaim his glory among the nations.
Did you know? The nations are described as bringing the people of Israel to Jerusalem as an offering to the LORD, using horses, chariots, litters, mules, and camels.
Did you know? The chapter speaks of a new heaven and a new earth and connects their enduring existence with the continued existence and name of Israel’s descendants.
Did you know? In the chapter’s vision of the future, all humanity will come to worship before the LORD from month to month and from Sabbath to Sabbath—a picture of worldwide worship of the LORD.

Did you know? The chapter ends with a stark contrast between those who serve the LORD and those who rebel against him: those leaving Jerusalem will see the corpses of the rebels, whose worm will not die and whose fire will not be quenched, and they will be an object of horror to all humanity.
